overview.eyebrow: Giving an established platform a bigger story
overview.lead: How do you bring AI into a product story without losing what people already love about it? That was the challenge behind Workvivo HQ.
overview.problem: Workvivo had earned its place in employee experience through connection, culture and adoption. As AI changed how people find information and get work done, the platform needed a broader ambition that still felt like Workvivo.
overview.contribution: I led the positioning and messaging architecture, connecting the platform story to the different priorities of IT, HR and Communications. I carried that thinking into the website and seller narrative, analyst framing and launch strategy, then built GTM kits and enabled Sales. The strategic choice was to make AI an expansion of Workvivo’s employee-experience strengths, connecting one platform story to distinct buying priorities.
overview.result: A coherent launch story that gave the platform room to grow while keeping employees at its centre. AI became part of the experience people already had a reason to use.
overview.learning: A bigger ambition works best when people can still recognise why they trusted you in the first place.

caseStudy.eyebrow: Repositioning a category for the AI era
caseStudy.context: Workvivo had established itself as an Employee Experience Platform. As enterprise software moved into an AI-native era, the challenge was bigger than adding AI features to the existing story: the company needed a credible new ambition without abandoning the employee-experience equity that made it distinctive.
caseStudy.challenge: What should Workvivo become when AI changes how employees interact with information, systems, and work? A generic ‘we’re now an AI company’ claim would have discarded the adoption, culture, frontline reach, and trust the platform had already earned.
caseStudy.insight: AI becomes more valuable when it lives inside an employee experience people already use. The platform story shifted toward an AI-native headquarters for every employee, captured in the central idea: Give work a home.

caseStudy.learning: Repositioning works when it expands what a brand can mean without erasing the reason customers trusted it in the first place.

overview.eyebrow: Keeping the story intact as more people and AI reuse it
overview.lead: AI makes messaging easier to create and distribute. I wanted to make it easier to reuse responsibly, too.
overview.problem: A message travels through decks, websites, launch kits and AI prompts. Along the way, its meaning, evidence or approval can get lost. I designed an operating model that keeps those connections visible and gives PMMs ownership of the words.
overview.contribution: I owned the project, wrote the messaging with support from my PMM team, and defined the content model, approval workflow and acceptance criteria. I directed AI-assisted implementation and tested changes and failures. Through testing, I moved the approach from a GitHub-based workflow to an in-house system using Zoom agents and Canvas, keeping the focus on an authoring experience the team could use.
overview.result: The HQ Agent pilot is complete and connected to our sales enablement agent, with positive feedback so far. Phase two is to write and test the remaining messaging. From there, the ambition is an agentic system connected to the design system, bringing governed messaging into content creation and automating more of the workflow.
overview.learning: The value is in turning messaging into a shared foundation for sales enablement, content creation and automation.

sections.title: The problem
paragraphs: Product messaging is reused across sales decks, launch materials, websites and AI prompts. Marketing, Sales and PMM need to adapt the story for different products, personas and assets while keeping claims accurate and the narrative consistent. Each adaptation creates another opportunity for wording to lose its context, evidence or approval status.

AI makes that content easier to produce and distribute. It also makes it more important to know which messages are current, supported and approved. I designed a structured messaging system to make reuse more reliable while preserving PMM ownership.

sections.title: My role and approach
paragraphs: I defined the content model, approval workflow and acceptance criteria, then directed AI-assisted implementation and tested how the system handled changes and failures. The model separates product facts from positioning, connects messages to their supporting sources, and gives content explicit ownership and review states.

The authoring pilot changed my approach. When the custom interface made it difficult to find and review the actual wording, I paused its expansion and prioritised familiar document editing, history and comments. Governance depends on people being able to understand and approve their own changes.

sections.title: How the system works
paragraphs: The intended change cycle is straightforward: a PMM edits wording, the system identifies the exact changes and checks them, and a human reviews the proposal before it becomes canonical. The implemented foundation prepares validated candidate changes and a receipt for review.
items: Edit: start from a known version of the message and submit the exact intended wording
Check: compare the edit with its baseline, preserve untouched fields and validate the candidate content
Review: retain the proposed change and its receipt for a human decision
Recover: stop when the underlying message has changed, so the author can compare versions and reconcile the edit
details: Typed objects separate product truth, buyer context, proof, messaging, design and asset recipes
Git records versions; Python and JSON Schema validate structure and references offline
An identity binding connects each authoring field to its canonical object; a deterministic compiler produces candidate files and a change receipt

sections.title: The decisions that mattered
items: Separate facts from positioning: product authority establishes what can be claimed; messaging determines how to communicate it for a buyer
Preserve exact edits: compile the wording the PMM submitted and leave other fields intact
Keep approval human: a successful technical check does not approve a claim or authorize publication
Make conflicts recoverable: preserve the original, submitted and current versions so the author can resolve a stale edit
Simplify authoring: prove one reliable change cycle in a familiar document workflow before adding more custom automation

sections.title: What I built and tested
paragraphs: The project produced a working foundation for validating structured messaging and proposing controlled changes for review. Development checks cover exact wording, untouched-field preservation, placeholders, stale edits, changed bindings and recovery from partial failures.

To make that behavior inspectable, I ran the existing compiler against a temporary local fixture using invented wording. One text edit produced a validated candidate and a change receipt. A separate comparison against a newer message returned STALE_AUTHORING_VIEW with no proposed changes.

sections.title: What I learned
paragraphs: The central design question was how to make messaging easier to reuse while keeping people accountable for its meaning and approval. The pilot showed that the collaboration experience is part of that governance: a technically controlled workflow still fails if the author cannot easily find and review the wording.
I would now prove the simplest complete human change cycle first, then add automation where it removes effort without obscuring ownership.

overview.eyebrow: Making enterprise AI make sense to the buyer
overview.lead: Search. An answer. A next step. HQ Agent needed a story that made that progression clear—and gave buyers a reason to care.
overview.problem: The product brought together enterprise knowledge, grounded answers and defined actions. Explaining the technology was only part of the job. Buyers also needed to understand where it fit, what they could trust and how to evaluate its value.
overview.contribution: I led product and portfolio positioning, translated technical detail into buyer value, and developed the seller narrative and enablement. I also co-developed pricing and packaging with the Revenue leader, connecting the commercial model to different levels of AI value. Understanding retrieval, grounding, permissions and connected actions helped me decide which promises we could credibly make and how to distinguish levels of value.
overview.result: A clear story built around search, answer and action, carried through positioning, packaging and launch. My role was to make the product understandable and commercially useful, working closely with the teams building it.
overview.learning: The strongest AI positioning connects product capability, buyer trust and a clear reason to choose.

caseStudy.context: HQ Agent extended Workvivo beyond communications and employee experience into trusted enterprise answers, search, self-service, and agentic task execution. It sat at the intersection of enterprise knowledge, RAG, permissions, employee experience, and Zoom’s broader AI technology.
caseStudy.challenge: The launch could not be reduced to ‘better enterprise search.’ It needed a clear category, a credible trust story, an understandable relationship with Workvivo HQ and ZoomMate, and sustainable packaging for different levels of AI value.
caseStudy.insight: The most useful commercial progression was SEARCH → ANSWER → ACTION: from finding information, to receiving a grounded answer, to increasingly completing the task. The launch idea became: From search, to answer, to job done.

caseStudy.learning: Technical depth matters in Product Marketing when it changes the claim, the value, the packaging, or the buyer’s trust.

caseStudy.eyebrow: Building an AI-enabled PMM operating model
caseStudy.context: AI-first Product Marketing is not simply a team using ChatGPT. Shauna has been exploring how AI can change the operating model of PMM itself—and where human judgment must remain accountable.
caseStudy.challenge: High-value PMM time disappears into retrieval, repeated seller questions, monitoring, synthesis, recurring research, and first-pass analysis. The strategic question is which work requires human judgment and which work can be processed or automated.
caseStudy.insight: AI does more of the processing. PMM remains accountable for the thinking. Retrieval, extraction, monitoring, classification, and repeatable analysis can accelerate; positioning, pricing, claims, category strategy, and executive recommendations still need accountable judgment.

overview.eyebrow: A portfolio you can have a conversation with
overview.lead: A case study can tell a story. A conversation can start with the part you actually care about. I wanted my portfolio to do both.
overview.problem: Recruiters, hiring managers and collaborators arrive with different questions. I wanted them to explore the work naturally, with answers that were specific, useful and faithful to my experience.
overview.contribution: I designed and integrated a voice and text agent on ElevenLabs, with a voice persona based on my own recordings. I shaped its personality, prompts, knowledge and routing, then tested different models and responses to improve clarity, relevance and accuracy.
overview.result: A live conversational layer for the portfolio. Visitors can ask about a project, a decision or my approach, while the agent draws on curated career and project material. The work brought voice design, product judgment and hands-on AI configuration together in one experience.
overview.learning: Designing the conversation means shaping what the agent knows, how it responds and why someone would want to use it.

caseStudy.eyebrow: Turning a résumé into an evidence-grounded conversation
caseStudy.context: A static portfolio can show the work, but it cannot adapt to the question a recruiter, hiring manager, or technical stakeholder actually wants answered. Shauna designed a live ElevenLabs experience that lets visitors explore her career, case studies, technical builds, and working principles through voice or text. She also created a voice persona from her own voice and gave the agent a defined personality so the experience feels recognisably hers without pretending to be her.
caseStudy.challenge: The agent needed to be persuasive without becoming a hype machine. It had to answer broad career questions quickly, go deep on named projects, distinguish work Shauna built from products she marketed, link back to public evidence, and avoid turning company outcomes or technical fluency into unsupported personal claims.
caseStudy.insight: A credible portfolio agent is a voice, context, workflow, and evaluation problem—not simply a prompt. Better answers came from defining the persona, separating durable rules from retrievable evidence, routing different intents to specialist answer modes, comparing model outputs, and analysing failures where attribution, role fit, or technical ownership could drift.

caseStudy.outcome: The result is a live, inspectable portfolio interface that demonstrates more than familiarity with AI tools. It shows Shauna's ability to shape a voice persona, engineer prompts, build an intent-routing workflow, configure retrieval and guardrails, compare model behaviour, analyse tests, and translate the technical decisions into a clear professional story. The agent runs on ElevenLabs; Shauna designed, configured, tested, documented, and integrated the experience rather than engineering the underlying voice models or platform runtime.
caseStudy.learning: The quality of an agent is shaped less by the cleverness of one prompt than by the discipline of its context, routing, evidence, evaluation, and boundaries.

overview.eyebrow: Building an analyst programme that could scale with the business
overview.lead: When our analyst-relations owner left, PMM absorbed the responsibility. I built a programme that made a substantial new remit manageable—and gave it room to grow.
overview.problem: Analyst relations meant much more than keeping briefings in the diary. PMM was taking on research submissions, executive narratives, customer proof and ongoing analyst engagement, alongside an already demanding product-marketing remit. We needed a programme that could scale as Workvivo and its portfolio evolved.
overview.contribution: I built a connected programme around analyst narrative, briefings and RFIs, evidence and customer-proof development, and alignment across the portfolio. I brought those activities together with competitive positioning, campaigns and seller enablement, so the work could build from one report cycle to the next.
overview.result: A scalable programme that sustained and continued to strengthen Workvivo’s leadership across reports, alongside recognition from Gartner, Forrester, G2, ClearBox and other analyst and review platforms. The team could support a growing programme within PMM and carry that market credibility into buyer and seller conversations.
overview.learning: A strong programme makes each report cycle build on the last, so the work and its value keep growing.

caseStudy.context: Workvivo evolved from an underdog employee app into a recognised Employee Experience Platform and later a broader AI-native employee-experience story. Analyst understanding had to evolve with the product and company narrative.
caseStudy.challenge: Market leadership is not created by a single briefing. It requires a consistent point of view, credible evidence, strong customer proof, disciplined claims, and alignment across products that are evolving at different speeds.
caseStudy.insight: Analyst relations works best as a connected category system—not a calendar of submissions. The analyst narrative, evidence base, competitive position, customer proof, and GTM story need to reinforce one another.

overview.lead: Collecting feedback is one thing. Helping an organisation do something useful with it is a much more interesting promise.
overview.problem: Seer took Workvivo into people intelligence. To earn attention in an established market, it needed a story that went beyond surveys and explained the gap between what employees say and what organisations act on.
overview.contribution: I led positioning and GTM strategy, launch planning, pricing and packaging, competitive framing and the seller narrative. I also hired a dedicated PMM to scale execution while retaining senior strategy ownership.
overview.result: A people-intelligence story organised around listen, understand and act. The Listening Gap gave it a memorable tension, connecting employee feedback and AI-assisted insight to the decisions leaders and managers need to make.
overview.learning: An adjacent market becomes a credible next step when you make the buyer’s problem—and your reason to solve it—clear.

caseStudy.context: Workvivo expanded into People Intelligence with Seer, moving into a buyer and category conversation adjacent to its employee-experience strengths.
caseStudy.challenge: Seer could not sound like another survey platform. The story needed to explain how employee feedback moves beyond collection—turning large volumes of qualitative signal into insight that leaders and managers can act on.
caseStudy.insight: The narrative became LISTEN → UNDERSTAND → ACT. The Listening Gap gave the strategy a memorable tension: organisations often collect employee feedback, but struggle to convert what they hear into meaningful action.

decisions: Anchor the story in action—not survey collection

caseStudy.outcome: Seer established a people-intelligence expansion story spanning employee listening, AI-assisted insight, manager intelligence, and action. No unverified Seer revenue or adoption metrics are claimed.
caseStudy.learning: Adjacent-market entry becomes credible when the narrative explains both the new capability and why the existing brand has earned the right to compete.

overview.eyebrow: Making a messaging review more useful, sooner
overview.lead: “This needs to be stronger” is easy feedback to give and hard feedback to use. I wanted a review that helped someone decide what to change next.
overview.problem: IT buyers read with different responsibilities and levels of context. A CIO, an architect and an internal champion can have very different questions about the same message. A useful review needs to recognise that.
overview.contribution: I defined the buyer lenses, review experience and evidence criteria, then used ChatGPT and Codex to prototype and develop the tool. I replaced a manual-first rubric with immediate feedback, priority changes and an editable rewrite brief, and tested how the scoring and source passages behaved.
overview.result: A live browser tool that turns positioning judgment into practical editing guidance. It shows the passages behind its feedback and helps the author shape the next draft. The score is an aid to judgment; it does not verify claims or replace a buyer’s response.
overview.learning: Good feedback gives someone a useful next move.

caseStudy.eyebrow: From a manual QA rubric to a buyer-focused decision aid
caseStudy.context: Positioning reviews often produce broad opinions rather than specific, actionable questions. The original AI Positioning QA made a rubric inspectable, but asking reviewers to complete eight dimensions created too much work before they received useful feedback.
caseStudy.challenge: Make the review immediately useful for enterprise IT messaging while retaining traceability. A CIO, an architecture lead and an internal champion can read the same asset with different responsibilities; an awareness asset should not be judged as a procurement brief.
caseStudy.insight: Start with the buyer’s remit and the job of the message. Surface the questions that matter next, show the source passages behind the diagnosis, and leave the claim and publication decision with a human.
contribution: Defined the IT-buyer scope, review experience and evidence standard
Directed AI-assisted prototyping in ChatGPT and implementation in Codex
Shaped six audience lenses, distinct buying roles and stage-aware review guidance
Pressure-tested scoring, source traceability, export behavior and input changes
Integrated the live tool, documentation and visual identity into this portfolio
decisions: Separate awareness stage from purchase stage: what the reader knows differs from what the buying group is deciding
Replace the manual-first interface with Gut Reaction, priority changes and buyer questions
Keep deep review inside the app with matching passages and an editable rewrite brief
Keep an inspectable /100 structural score with explicit stage weights, separate proof status and visible critical-claim warnings
Keep the public tool vendor-neutral and retain the original eight-dimension manual evaluator as a separate workflow
architecture: Static HTML and CSS provide the interface; vanilla JavaScript runs locally in the browser
Pure modules separate six IT buyer profiles and rewrite guidance from the versioned 0–4 scoring rubric
The UI module renders source excerpts, prioritised questions, stage guidance and the rewrite brief
Markdown export preserves the source, context, supplied proof and edited rewrite; the app makes no model or network calls
The portfolio hosts a versioned copy of the public runtime, with a source commit and file hashes recorded in its manifest
tooling: ChatGPT for prototype iteration and Codex for integration, refactoring and checks
Node’s test runner for deterministic scoring and export tests
GitHub for version control and GitHub Pages for static hosting
Generated case-study artwork; interface styling follows the portfolio palette
safeguards: Supplied proof is displayed as unverified context and cannot inflate the score of the source copy
Edits invalidate displayed results and exports; source HTML is escaped rather than executed
Quoted passages preserve the original source whitespace
No automatic saving, tracking or external model calls in the tool
Private research attachments are not published; unsupported research percentages were withheld
validation: 59 automated checks passed for rubric 3.1, retaining the original manual-evaluator tests
Checks cover proof isolation, citations, selected negation cases, vendor substitutions, proposed measurements, risk flags and all 54 remit/role/stage combinations
Browser checks covered compact results, deep review, edited-brief export, escaped HTML, stale-result invalidation and 320px/390px layouts
Semantic relationships, unusual phrasing and unverified evidence remain limitations; independent human calibration has not been completed
caseStudy.outcome: A live IT messaging review that gives immediate, inspectable guidance and a reusable rewrite brief. The build demonstrates how positioning judgment can become a practical workflow. It does not establish commercial lift, buyer agreement or production-grade approval governance.
caseStudy.learning: A useful review system must make its limits as visible as its recommendations. Simplifying the interface only helps if the evidence and the human decision remain clear.
